study.title: Numbers 35 - Cities for Levites and justice for murder
study.overview: The chapter organizes two things linked to the sanctity of the land of Israel: the distribution of cities for the Levites and the creation of cities of refuge for cases of accidental death. The Levites do not receive a tribal territory of their own, but cities scattered among the other tribes, which places them in the midst of the people. At the same time, God clearly distinguishes between intentional murder and unintentional death, preserving the life of the involuntary guilty without weakening justice against murder. The chapter ends with the theological reason of all this: the land must not be contaminated by shed blood, because the Lord himself dwells in the midst of Israel.

outline.title: Inheritance of the Levites among the tribes
outline.explanation: God commands the Levites to receive cities with their fields around, and not a territorial inheritance of their own like the other tribes. Cities must be distributed in proportion to the size of the inheritance of each tribe, showing a balanced sharing of the people of Israel.

outline.title: The cities of refuge and the difference between accident and crime
outline.explanation: The Lord establishes six cities of refuge, open to the foreigner who lives among Israel. The text defines signs of voluntary homicide - such as the use of weapon, hatred and ambush - and separates these cases from accidental death, which must be judged by the congregation.

outline.title: Temporary protection and limits of justice
outline.explanation: Whoever has killed without intention must remain in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, and cannot be redeemed for payment. There is also a requirement of witnesses and an express refusal to accept a price for the life of the homicide or for the restriction imposed on the refugee.

outline.title: Blood contaminates the land where God dwells
outline.explanation: The chapter concludes by stating that the shedding of blood profanes the earth and that guilt is not removed by simple tolerance. The judicial order exists because the Lord dwells in the midst of his people; therefore, the holiness of the earth and coexistence depends on real justice.

study.context: The text is located in the fields of Moab, by the Jordan of Jericho, at the end of the desert journey. The notes provided highlight that the Levites did not receive their own territory, but scattered cities among the tribes, and that this placed them in the midst of the people with spiritual influence. They also note that the system of cities of refuge preserves an ancient logic of revenge from the relative, but submits it to community judgment and the distinction between accidental death and deliberate murder.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that human life belongs to God and cannot be treated lightly. Biblical justice is not uncontrolled revenge or indulgence without criterion: it protects the innocent, punishes the guilty and requires public assessment of the facts. The city of refuge shows mercy to the involuntary murder, but this mercy does not cancel the seriousness of the death caused. The shed blood pollutes the land because the Lord dwells in the midst of his people; thus divine holiness reaches both worship and the judicial system. There is also a principle of equality, because the same norm applies to Israelis and to the resident foreigner.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter shows that the Levites did not receive their own territory, but cities scattered among the other tribes, to live among the people and exert spiritual influence.

The note provided does not directly comment on this chapter; it deals with the narrative unfolding in the following chapter, dealing with the issue of Zelophedehad's daughters and the regulation of inheritance in the family.

The cities of refuge were for those who killed unintentionally, and they were different from places of asylum that protected guilty; in them the innocent was preserved without abolishing the punishment of the homicide.

questions: How does the distinction between accidental death and intentional murder correct both impulsive revenge and impunity?
What does it mean, in practice, that God dwells in the midst of his people and therefore the earth should not be contaminated?
In what ways can the church today protect life and at the same time act with mercy and justice?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to honor human life and treat conflicts with truth, trials and responsibility. Avoid hasty trials, but also do not minimize guilt or violence. At home, in the church and at work, practice a justice that listens before concluding, protects the vulnerable and does not turn mercy into permission for evil. Remember that God's holiness also reaches the way we deal with offenses, accusations and conflicts.
study.uncertainty: Notes provided to Matthew Henry do not deal directly with Numbers 35, but the following chapter, so the pointing attributed to this source is necessarily contextual and limited. There is also a note in the notes on the measurement of the fields around the cities that was discussed by commentators, but the text and notes do not definitively resolve the apparent tension between the mentioned measures. No external data on geography, dating or history have been added beyond what is explicitly in the given notes.
